conflicts.note: There is no documentary evidence in the Rolex patent of co-development with Doxa. Urs Eschle's claim of a shared patent appears unsupported. Useful as a 'sea-dweller' / 'comex' context note rather than as a 5512/5513 claim.
positions: Standard Rolex narrative (Monochrome, Bob's Watches, Rolex's own materials): Rolex invented and patented the HEV, with the patent filed 6 November 1967 (inventor André Zibach) and granted June 1970.

Perezcope's 2025 update: Doxa demonstrated a working HEV prototype at Comex's hyperbaric centre during 'Ludion 2' (15–28 November 1967) — just 9 days after Rolex's patent filing — and the Doxa Sub 300 Conquistador was shown publicly in April 1968, suggesting Doxa was at least parallel and possibly ahead in prototyping, though Rolex secured the patent.
conflicts.topic: Who invented the helium-escape valve first

conflicts.note: The corpus's only primary-sourced figure is the Rolex-cited 1:10. The 1:20 figure remains common in market-facing writing.
positions: Rolex's own 2024 publication cites 17,338 (5512) vs 151,449 (5513), i.e. roughly 1:10.
Older market lore (cited by Charlie Dunne / Hodinkee) traditionally estimated about 1:20.

conflicts.note: All sources agree the 6200 has a lower number but appeared chronologically after the 6204; the dispute is about which was developed/produced first internally.
positions: Most historians (Monochrome, Hodinkee, Bob's Watches) treat the 6204 as the first Submariner (early-1953 / II.53 caseback stamps), with the 6200 'King Sub' coming after despite its lower number.
Rolex Passion Market and Rolex Magazine suggest the 6200 was likely the first physically produced but held back commercially in favour of the slimmer 6204 launched at Basel 1954.
conflicts.topic: 6204 vs 6200 — which was the first Submariner

conflicts.note: Not a factual conflict so much as a tonal one — useful for the demand-story / cultural-context section.
positions: Teddy Baldassarre and Hodinkee frame the 5513 as Rolex's quintessential approachable tool watch, especially in matte-dial form.

Fratello observes the modern Submariner has shifted toward luxury/'wrist-flex' territory, and Bob's Watches notes the 1980s glossy/white-gold-surround dials as the first hint of luxury creep into the 5513 itself.
conflicts.topic: Whether the 5512/5513 are 'tool watches' or have become luxury items

consensus.claim: The Submariner debuted in 1953–54, with Rolex officially considering 1953 the birth year (first production cases) and the public unveiling at the 1954 Basel Fair.

René-Paul Jeanneret, a Rolex director and keen diver who was close to Jacques-Yves Cousteau, is credited with championing the concept of a sporty-yet-elegant waterproof watch that became the Submariner.
At launch the Submariner was promoted as waterproof to 100m, with the Blancpain Fifty Fathoms (rated to roughly 91m) preceding it to market by a few months in 1953.
The 5512 (introduced 1959) was the first Submariner with crown guards and established the 40mm Oyster case that has defined the model ever since.

The 5512 and 5513 are mechanically and visually near-identical except that, from about 1962 onward, the 5512 carried a chronometer-certified movement (and the additional 'Superlative Chronometer Officially Certified' dial text) while the 5513 used a non-chronometer calibre.
The 5513 ran from 1962 until roughly 1989, making it one of the longest-produced Submariner references and the model many collectors first picture when imagining a vintage Sub.
The 5513 used the calibre 1530 early on and later the simpler, non-chronometer calibre 1520, both running at 19,800 vph after 1965.
5512s used calibre 1530 (1959–1962), then chronometer-grade 1560 (c.1962–1965), then 1570 (c.1965–1979/80), with hacking added to the 1570 in the early 1970s.
Rolex's own 2024 publication cites total production of 17,338 examples of the 5512 versus 151,449 examples of the 5513 — roughly a 1:10 ratio.

5512 and 5513 dials evolved through three broad eras: glossy gilt dials (early 1960s to roughly 1967), matte dials (c.1967 to c.1984), and glossy black dials with white-gold-surrounded markers (c.1984 to end of production).
The matte-dial 5513 sequence proceeded from Meters First (c.1966) → non-serif/serif dials → 'Pre-COMEX' → Maxi I through Maxi V, ending around 1984 when the glossy white-gold-surround dial arrived.

Within the 5513, named dial variants collectors track include the gilt 'Explorer-dial' (c.1962–1965, with 3/6/9 Arabic numerals), 'underline' and 'double-Swiss underline' dials, and the 'Bart Simpson' dial (so named for the shape of the coronet).

The 5513 'MilSub' was supplied to the British Ministry of Defence in the early–mid 1970s with fixed lug bars, a sword/baton minute hand, a circled-T tritium marker, and a fully graduated 60-minute bezel; the dedicated 5517 succeeded it later in the decade, with double-reference 5513/5517 examples known.

The 1680 (1969–1979) introduced the date with cyclops to the Submariner; early dials carry 'Submariner' in red ('Red Sub') and the model was the first Submariner offered in solid 18k yellow gold (ref. 1680/8, 1969).

Rolex partnered with COMEX from around 1970–71, supplying watches in exchange for real-world saturation-diving feedback; COMEX received 5513s, 5514s, 1680s and Sea-Dwellers, with the dedicated 5514 (no-date Submariner case fitted with a gas-escape valve) being COMEX-specific.

The helium/gas-escape valve was patented by Rolex (filed 6 November 1967, granted June 1970, inventor André Zibach) and is associated with the Sea-Dweller (1665) and COMEX-spec watches; the standard Submariner 5512/5513 was never produced for civilian sale with a gas-escape valve.

Sean Connery's Bond wore a Big-Crown Submariner (commonly identified as the 6538) in Dr. No (1962), From Russia with Love (1963) and Goldfinger (1964), cementing the Submariner's place in popular culture.

Roger Moore's Bond wore a 5513 in Live and Let Die (1973), The Man with the Golden Gun and On Her Majesty's Secret Service, and a screen-used 5513 prop modified by production designer Syd Cain with a fictional buzz-saw bezel/magnetic gadgetry — caseback signed 'Roger Moore 007' — has been documented at auction.

The 5513 was succeeded by the 14060 in 1989/1990, which introduced the unidirectional bezel to the no-date Submariner; ceramic Cerachrom bezels and the larger 'Super Case' arrived with the 114060 in 2010, and the case grew to 41mm with the 124060 in 2020.

Vintage Submariner Oyster bracelets evolved through three broad generations: rivet bracelets (e.g. 7206/6636 and US-made C&I) in the early 1960s, folded-link 9315 in the late 1960s through 1970s, and solid-link 93150 in the 1980s; Gay Frères was the principal supplier.

marks.explanation: Earliest matte 5513 dial style (c.1966–1969), so-named because the depth rating reads '200m=660ft' with metres before feet. Transition begins around the 1.6m serial range.
marks.name: Meters First (5513 matte)

marks.explanation: Matte 5513 dial style from c.1969 onward in which the depth rating reads '660ft=200m'. Aligned with US-market production scaling.
marks.name: Feet First (5513 matte)

marks.explanation: 5513 matte dial with fat coronet and 'SUBMARINER' printed below the depth rating; named by Ed Delgado in 2008 for sharing print characteristics with some 5514 COMEX dials. Distinct from Maxi I by coronet shape and 'S' style.
marks.name: Pre-COMEX dial

marks.explanation: Five successive 5513 matte dials (c.1977–1984) with progressively larger tritium plots and shifting positions of 'SUBMARINER', depth rating and the '=' sign; distinguishable by coronet taper, serif/non-serif 'f', open 6s, and presence of the 'zig-zag S'.
marks.name: Maxi I–V dials

marks.explanation: Gilt 5513 dial (c.1962–1965) with 3/6/9 Arabic numerals, echoing the 6200 'King Sub' configuration. The last Explorer-dial Submariner and among the most sought-after.
marks.name: Explorer dial 5513

marks.explanation: 5513 dial nickname for a coronet shape that evokes Bart Simpson's hair.
marks.name: Bart Simpson dial

marks.explanation: Transitional gilt 5512/5513 dials carrying a printed underline beneath the depth-rating text, used by Rolex to flag tritium-vs-radium changeovers.
marks.name: Underline / Double-Swiss Underline

marks.explanation: 5513 (and later 5517) supplied to the British MoD in the 1970s with fixed lug bars, sword/baton minute hand, circled-T tritium marker, and a 60-minute fully graduated bezel. Double-stamped 5513/5517 examples exist.
marks.name: MilSub

marks.explanation: A single known factory-blacked-out (teflon-coated, gunmetal) 5513 made in 1975 for the South African Special Forces during Operation Savannah; verified by Rolex Patrimoine.
marks.name: The Shadow

marks.explanation: 1680 with 'Submariner' printed in red on a four-line gilt or matte dial; six dial Marks (MkI–MkVI plus a MkVII Luminova service dial) are catalogued.
marks.name: Red Sub (1680)

marks.explanation: Gold 1680/8 (and 16808) dial with raised conical 'nipple' hour markers, in black or blue; the blue variants are prone to dramatic patina (purple, green, brown, turquoise).
marks.name: Nipple dial 1680/8

marks.explanation: Big-Crown 6538 worn by Sean Connery in Dr. No, From Russia with Love and Goldfinger; widely identified as the original on-screen James Bond watch.
marks.name: Bond Sub (6538)

marks.explanation: Screen-used 5513 prop from Live and Let Die (1973), modified by production designer Syd Cain with a fictional spinning buzz-saw bezel and magnetic field; caseback signed 'Roger Moore 007'. Sold by Phillips, Geneva.
marks.name: Roger Moore 'Q' 5513

model_context: The Rolex Submariner is widely regarded as the archetypal modern dive watch and one of the most culturally pervasive sports watches ever produced. It emerged from the post-war boom in recreational scuba diving — propelled by Cousteau and Gagnan's Aqua-Lung — and from the vision of René-Paul Jeanneret, a Rolex director and keen diver who pushed the brand to build a sporty-yet-elegant waterproof watch. Rolex draws on its 1926 Oyster case and 1931 Perpetual rotor as the technical foundation. The first models appeared in 1953–54, with a 1953 Deep Sea Special strapped to Auguste Piccard's Bathyscaphe descending to 3,131.8m serving as the launch's marketing centrepiece. The 5512 (1959) introduced crown guards and the 40mm case that became the modern blueprint; the 5513 (1962–1989) ran alongside it as the non-chronometer sibling and became the longest-running, most-produced classic Submariner — the watch most people picture when they think 'Submariner'. The model line later branched into the date-equipped 1680, the gold 1680/8, the saturation-diving Sea-Dweller (1665), MilSub/COMEX variants, and the modern 14060/114060/124060 lineage. Demand was driven by Bond, professional diver use (COMEX, SEALAB, Tektite), and the watch's transcendence of its tool-watch origins into a near-default luxury sport watch.

module_candidates.rationale: Two distinct Bond stories — Connery's 6538 in Dr. No / FRWL / Goldfinger, and Moore's 5513 in Live and Let Die etc., plus the Syd Cain 'Q' 5513 prop — deserve their own page with auction provenance from Phillips, Christie's and Bonhams.

The corpus has rich, primary-source material on the Rolex–COMEX partnership from 1970/71, the prototype 5513 with HEV, and the dedicated 5514. Deserves a standalone page so it doesn't crowd a 5512/5513 reference page.
Distinct British MoD-issue feature set (fixed bars, sword hands, T-circle, fully graduated bezel) plus the 'Shadow' South African outlier and the Licence to Kill prop — a clear dedicated topic.

module_candidates.module: Sea-Dweller and the Gas Escape Valve
module_candidates.rationale: The 1665 / Single Red / Double Red / 16660 / Doxa controversy is a complete narrative arc that overlaps with but is distinct from the Submariner — and Perezcope's deep research deserves a home that won't muddy the Sub page.
VRFM provides a deep, self-contained collector's guide including dial Marks, weights, gold value and alloy evolution — a natural standalone page.
VRFM's MkI–MkVII taxonomy of Red Sub dials is granular enough to warrant its own page.
The rivet → folded-link 9315 → solid-link 93150 evolution, plus Gay Frères/C&I suppliers, is a transversal topic that applies to multiple Sub references.
The 5513mattedial.com material on Maxi I–V is highly specialised and could be a dedicated sub-page off the 5513.

source_contributions.unique_contribution: Granular taxonomy of 5513 Maxi I–V matte dials with diagnostic features (coronet shape, 'zig-zag S', position of '=' in depth rating, serif/non-serif 'f', open 6s, relative length of SUBMARINER vs depth rating) and approximate serial/year ranges.
Canonical chronological sequence of 5513 matte dial families (Meters First → Non-serif/Serif → Pre-COMEX → Maxi I–V) and the etymology of 'Pre-COMEX' from Ed Delgado's 2008 VRF post.
Framing of the 5513 matte dial era (c.1966–1984) and acknowledgement of Tomvox's foundational Maxi-dial research.
Detailed walk-through of 6204/6205/6200/6536/6538 early references, including the Sub-Aqua UK-market dial, split-logo variants, and the introduction of Mercedes hands and the 8mm Brevet Big Crown.

Bridges 5508/5510 to 5512/5513/1680, including the 5508 being the first Submariner to use tritium (vs radium) and the last without crown guards, and the rationale for the 1680 date complication being prompted by the Sea-Dweller.
Patent-level forensic on the Rolex HEV (CH492246, inventor André Zibach, filed Nov 1967), and the T. Walker Lloyd / Bob Barth origin story of the valve concept.

Documents retrofitting of the GEV onto 1.6m-serial Single Red Sea-Dwellers given to SEALAB 3, Tektite 1 and Deepstar 4000 personnel — and notes that 5512s were also gifted at the Deepstar 500-dive ceremony.

Origin of the 'Gas Escape Valve' wording — chosen because Brauer's Hydra programme involved hydrogen as well as helium — and that 'Patent Pending' engravings were punch-stamped in the same fashion as 1953 Everest Pre-Explorers.

The South African Special Forces teflon-coated 5513 'Shadow' (case ~4.093m, 1975) verified by Rolex Patrimoine, with the Operation Savannah context, and noting the watch inspired the later Bamford and Pro Hunter blackout customisations.

Newly-surfaced evidence (Comex 'Ludion 2', 15–28 Nov 1967; Swiss press April 1968) suggesting Doxa had a working HEV prototype just 9 days after Rolex filed its patent — complicating the Rolex-first narrative.

Long enumeration of dial-printing micro-variants across 6200/6204/6205/6536/6536-1/5508/5510/5512/5513 (minute-track types, tulip vs square crowns, gold/white Swiss, double-name retailer signatures) and an emphasis on the demand context after Everest/Piccard.

Personal-provenance vignette of a 1967 Meters-First 5513 found in a desk drawer and serviced by Rolex in 2003 with then-current parts (Luminova, white-gold surrounds), illustrating how Rolex servicing transforms vintage watches.
Notes that Rolex assembled WWII Panerai Radiomir cases/movements for the Italian Navy, and that Blancpain's patent on the unidirectional dive bezel kept Rolex on bidirectional bezels until the 1980s.

First-person letter from a former British Royal Navy / COMEX diver ('Stuart L.') accompanying a 1971 2.8m-serial 5513 retrofitted with a prototype HEV — a rare documented civilian-issued 5513 with HEV outside the 5514 reference.
Compact Submariner timeline (1953/1959/1967/1969/1979/1984/1988/2003/2010/2020) with the Twinlock crown technical detail and 1953 Cannes Institute test report citation (132 dives, 12–60m).
Lot essay for the Live and Let Die 5513 prop, describing Q's fictional magnetised buzz-saw bezel and its on-screen uses.
On-wrist observation that the 124060/126610LN bezel reflects less light than the 116610 generation, and that the 41mm case wears closer to 40.5mm in practice.
Places the modern Submariner alongside its lateral peers (Fifty Fathoms, Seamaster Diver 300M, Doxa Sub 300, Panerai Submersible, Tudor BB) for category context.
Highlights the brief (~9-month, 1988–89) ref. 168000 'Triple Zero' transition to 904L steel as a sleeper collector reference.
Sets out the tritium-vs-Luminova cutoff (1998) and Super-LumiNova (2000) within the 14060/14060M, and notes the 16610LV ('Kermit') five distinct dial/bezel sub-variants over 2003–2010.

Quotes Geneva specialist Sacha Davidoff comparing the Submariner's incremental evolution to the Porsche 911 and consolidates the catalogue of modern nicknames (Kermit, Hulk, Smurf, Triple Zero, Bond Sub).

Practical 5513 buying-guide framing including Oyster bracelet generations (rivet → folded-link 9315 → solid-link 93150), Gay Frères/C&I supplier note, and Charlie Dunne quote on the 1:20 perceived 5512:5513 ratio (vs Rolex's 1:10).
Reference-by-reference scholarly treatment of every four-digit Sub, including the 6204 II.53 caseback stamp, the 'clean dial' 6205 series, the 'King Sub' 6200 nickname, and bezel/handset evolution.
Confirms the Bond/Rolex connection extends into Ian Fleming's original novels and tracks notable auction appearances of Bond-associated 6538s and 5513s.
Authoritative auction catalogue entry for the Live and Let Die screen-used 5513 prop, including the Syd Cain biographical context as designer of Bond's on-screen Rolex gadgetry.
1958 Rolex brochure showing a 6536 without depth rating and describing the 6538 as the heavy-duty version, plus the brochure's spelling 'sub-marine' suggesting period pronunciation 'Sub-marine-er'.
Photographic evidence of Cousteau testing Submariner prototypes in 1953 and Chuck Yeager / Elvis / Brian Kelly (Flipper) wearing Big Crown Subs — useful for cultural-history detail.

Material analysis of the 18k gold Submariners (~185g, ~138.75g pure gold), evolution of the blue nipple-dial 1680/8 patinas (purple, green, brown, turquoise), and the case-making supply chain (Genex/Gay Frères, Boninchi, Virex et Joli Poli).
Maps the Red 1680 dial families: Meters-first MkI–III, Feet-first MkIV–VI, and the MkVII Luminova service dial, attributing manufacture to Singer, Beyler, Stern and Lemrich.
Places the Submariner within the broader dive-watch firmament alongside the Fifty Fathoms, Seamaster 300, Doxa Sub 300T, Ploprof, and Sea-Dweller / Deepsea Challenge.

The single most authoritative 5512 reference piece in the corpus: 1959–1980 production span, calibre transitions (1530→1560→1570), and citation of Rolex's own 2024 production figures (17,338 vs 151,449).

stories.title: Jeanneret, Cousteau and the birth of the Submariner
stories.why: The founding human story — a Rolex director and diver, friends with Cousteau, persuades the board to build a sporty waterproof watch. Anchors the model-wide origin section.

stories.title: Piccard's Bathyscaphe and the 1953 Deep Sea Special
stories.why: The marketing stunt that announced Rolex's deep-water credentials: a specially built Rolex strapped to the outside of Piccard's bathyscaphe descending 3,131.8m, returning unscathed, just as the consumer Submariner was about to be launched.

stories.title: Connery's 6538 and the original Bond watch
stories.why: The single most important pop-culture moment for the early Submariner; recurs across nearly every source as the watch that made the Sub culturally inescapable.

stories.title: The Roger Moore 'Q' 5513 — Live and Let Die
stories.why: A genuinely distinctive 5513-specific Bond story: a screen-used 5513 modified by Syd Cain with a fictional buzz-saw bezel and magnetic field, caseback engraved 'Roger Moore 007', sold by Phillips.

stories.title: 'The Shadow' — South African Special Forces 5513
stories.why: The only known factory-blacked-out Rolex: a 1975 5513 in gunmetal teflon coating, made for South African special forces during Operation Savannah, later confirmed by Rolex Patrimoine. Inspired the entire blacked-out custom Sub genre (Bamford, Pro Hunter).

stories.title: Stuart L.'s 1971 COMEX 5513 prototype
stories.why: A documented civilian-issued 5513 (2.8m serial, 1971) retrofitted with a prototype HEV and used in commercial deep diving — provenance via a letter from the original Royal Navy / COMEX diver. Concrete evidence that some 5513s left the factory with valves before the dedicated 5514.

stories.title: Steve McQueen's 5512/5513
stories.why: Often misremembered as an Explorer II story, McQueen actually wore a Submariner — Wind Vintage and GQ both note the 5512 as his Sub of choice, which underpins much of the watch's mid-century cool-factor.

stories.title: Teddy's father's 1982 Feet-First 5513 and grandfather's 1967 Meters-First 5513
stories.why: A real-life illustration of how Rolex servicing in the early 2000s could transform a Meters-First matte 5513 into something resembling a late 1989 model (Luminova, white-gold surrounds, no tritium) — a cautionary tale about originality and dial integrity.

stories.title: Cousteau testing Submariner prototypes in 1953
stories.why: Photographic evidence cited by Rolex Magazine ties the model's earliest prototypes to Cousteau personally, reinforcing the Jeanneret/Cousteau founding myth.

stories.title: Chuck Yeager and Elvis in Big-Crown Subs
stories.why: Brief but evocative cultural anchors for the pre-5512 era — Yeager (1956) and Elvis (1962) photographed wearing 6538s.
